The menu opens by pressing Space, Up arrow, or Down arrow, and closes by pressing Space or Enter to select an item.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (What Carbon provides > Pagination nav).

author: IBM
title: Pagination
statement: Not all the elements in pagination have static or visually isolated labels. Carbon constructs a programmatic name for the second select by concatenating dynamically generated text on the screen. Carbon also provides accessible names for the icon-only buttons. Carbon provides the accessible names "Page", "Previous", and "Next" for assistive technology.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (What Carbon provides > Pagination).

author: IBM
subcategory: Pagination > What Carbon provides > Pagination nav
title: Pagination: Pagination nav
statement: Carbon constructs a programmatic name for the page ghost buttons by concatenating dynamically generated text on the screen. Carbon also provides accessible names for the icon-only buttons. Carbon provides the accessible names "Page", "Previous", and "Next" for assistive technology.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (What Carbon provides > Pagination nav).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - Carbon uses elements for the dropdowns. - Consult the ARIA authoring practices for more considerations.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Pagination
statement: Pagination splits content or data into several pages, with a control for navigating to the next or previous page. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Pagination Pagination nav Modifiers Related Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" ().

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Overview
statement: Pagination organizes and divides large amounts of content on separate pages and gives the user control over how much content they want to view on each page. Pagination can be used with a data table or on a page. Example of the pagination component in a UI
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Overview).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: When to use
statement: - When it could take a considerable amount of time to load the available data at once or in a scrolling view - When there is too much data to display on one page or within one view of a component - To make large amounts of data more accessible to consume by users - To optimize on-page real estate - To give users more control over how they view large amounts of information
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Overview > When to use).

author: IBM
subcategory: Pagination > Overview > When not to use
title: Pagination: When not to use
statement: - Do not use it to display linear journeys, for example, in a form progression. Instead, use the progress bar or button components to navigate forward and backward. - Do not use pagination superfluously, and aim to use it to improve usability or performance.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Overview > When not to use).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Variants
statement: ; Variant ; Usage ; ; Pagination ; The pagination variant is typically connected at the bottom of the data table component to help paginate large amounts of data.; Pagination nav; The pagination nav variant is mainly used in on-page situations to help paginate either a whole page or sections of a page. ;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Overview > Variants).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Anatomy of pagination
statement: Anatomy of the pagination variant 1. Items per page: Shows the current number of items that appear per page. 2. Range of items: Shows the current range of items and lists the total amount of items. 3. Current page: Shows the current page the user is on and lists the total amount of pages. 4. Previous and next buttons: Buttons that take you to the previous or next page. 5. Container: The container bar of the whole pagination component.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Formatting > Anatomy of pagination).

author: IBM
subcategory: Pagination > Formatting > Anatomy of pagination nav
title: Pagination: Anatomy of pagination nav
statement: Anatomy of the pagination nav variant 1. Unselected page button: A page the user could select and view. 2. Selected page button: The current page the user is viewing. 3. Overflow button: Contains available pages that can be navigated to but cannot be shown upfront in the component because of the current viewport. 4. Previous and next buttons: Buttons that take you to the previous or next page. 5. Container: The container of the whole pagination component.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Formatting > Anatomy of pagination nav).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Sizing
statement: The pagination component is available in three sizes in both variants: large, medium, and small. Sizes of pagination Sizes of pagination nav
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Formatting > Sizing).

author: IBM
subcategory: Pagination > Formatting > Data table size pairings
title: Pagination: Data table size pairings
statement: We recommend using the same height pagination as you do for the data table component rows to which it is connected. In some cases, the height sizes of these two components will not be the same because we do not offer extra small and extra large sizes for pagination. When using the extra large data table row height, use the large pagination. When using the extra small data table row height, use the small pagination. Size pairings of the pagination and data table components
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Formatting > Data table size pairings).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Placement
statement: Place the pagination near the related component or area of the page where the information will be paginated.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Formatting > Placement).

author: IBM
subcategory: Pagination > Formatting > Placing pagination with data table
title: Pagination: Placing pagination with data table
statement: When using the pagination variant with a data table, the pagination should be stacked and below the table with no padding between them. Placement of the pagination variant
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Formatting > Placing pagination with data table).

author: IBM
subcategory: Pagination > Formatting > Placing pagination nav on a page
title: Pagination: Placing pagination nav on a page
statement: When using the pagination nav variant on a page, float it below the content to which it is paginating and related to. The pagination can be right aligned or left aligned to the content above it. When it doubt, choose right alignment. Placement of the pagination nav variant
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Formatting > Placing pagination nav on a page).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Label text
statement: The label text in the pagination component should be concise and instructional. It describes the items per page and the number of pages or items. We recommend not modifying the label text unless necessary for specific use cases.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Content > Label text).

author: IBM
subcategory: Pagination > Content > Select component option text
title: Pagination: Select component option text
statement: The select components option text is shown as a number, indicating the items per page and the current page. Alternatively, this can be indicated as a word for the “Items per page” selection instead of a number.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Content > Select component option text).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Overflow content
statement: In the pagination nav variant, an ellipsis button appears between pages to indicate that there are numerous pages to navigate to within the ellipsis button menu. We recommend never placing the ellipsis button at the beginning or end of a series of pages in the pagination component. Example of the ellipsis button for overflow content in the pagination nav variant
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Content > Overflow content).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Pagination
statement: The pagination variant is typically a bar attached to the bottom of a data table to paginate its data. Example of the pagination variant in a UI
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: States
statement: The pagination variant has the select component and ghost icon button component nested within it and inherits their component states. For more information on these states, refer to the select and ghost icon button style tab guidance.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination > States).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Mouse
statement: - Clicking on the select component will open the menu and reveal options. - To close the menu, choose a different option or click outside the menu area. - Clicking on a previous or next button will navigate you to the previous or next page.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination > Mouse).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Keyboard
statement: - On focus, the select component menu is opened with pressing Spaceor with Up or Down arrows which also cycle through the values. - Pressing Space orEnter selects a value and closes the menu. - The menu can be closed by pressing Esc. - The previous and next ghost icon buttons are activated by pressing Space or Enter.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination > Keyboard).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Responsive behavior
statement: The pagination variant retains all its content and nested components at every breakpoint except for the small breakpoint. The select components have been removed at the small breakpoint, but information on the total number of items, items being displayed, and previous and next buttons remain. Pagination variant responsive behavior in all breakpoints versus the small breakpoint
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination > Responsive behavior).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Clickable areas
statement: Within the pagination variant, there are four clickable areas. Two select components allow you to change the number of items per page and the page number. Two ghost icon buttons take you to the previous or next page. Pagination variant clickable areas
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination > Clickable areas).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Pagination nav
statement: The pagination nav variant is most commonly used to paginate full pages or sections of content on a page. It floats under and near the related content. Example of the pagination nav variant in a UI
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination nav).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: States
statement: The pagination nav variant has the ghost icon button component and the breadcrumb overflow button component nested within it that inherits their component states. For more information on these states, refer to the select and breadcrumb overflow button style tab guidance.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination nav > States).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Mouse
statement: - Clicking on a button number will navigate you to that page. - Clicking on a previous or next caret button will navigate you to the previous and next pages of the one you are currently viewing. - Clicking on an overflow ellipsis button will open a select menu to choose a page to navigate to. Upon clicking on a page option from the menu, you will navigate to that page.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination nav > Mouse).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Keyboard
statement: - The icon button receives focus and you can move between buttons by pressing the Up or Down arrows. - The page number buttons are activated by pressing Space or Enter. - The previous and next buttons are activated by pressing Space or Enter.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination nav > Keyboard).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Responsive behavior
statement: In small screens, the pagination nav variant can provide an ellipsis button to indicate there are more pages to navigate to within the ellipsis button menu. Pagination nav variant responsive behavior in large versus small breakpoints
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination nav > Responsive behavior).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Clickable areas
statement: Every button in the pagination nav variant is clickable. Two ghost icon buttons take you to the previous or next page. The rest of the page number buttons take you to that particular page. Clickable areas within the pagination nav variant
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Pagination nav > Clickable areas).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Page looping
statement: For the pagination nav variant, instead of turning off the previous or next caret buttons when you reach either the first or last page of the pagination component, you can enable the option to loop through the available pages continuously.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Modifiers > Page looping).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Page naming
statement: By default, the select component option text is displayed as a number, showing items per page and the current page. However, we offer an alternative option to use a word instead of a number for the “Items per page” selection if that better meets your requirements. Select components content alternative of numbers versus words
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Modifiers > Page naming).

author: IBM
title: Pagination: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Pagination" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Popover
statement: No accessibility annotations are needed for popover, but keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. What Carbon provides Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" ().

author: IBM
title: Popover: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via the keyboard. Carbon incorporates many other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Popover > What Carbon provides > Keyboard interactions
title: Popover: Keyboard interactions
statement: Popovers use an icon button for the trigger. These buttons are in the tab order and are activated by pressing Enter or Space. The activation toggles the popover open and closed, and focus remains on the trigger. When the popover contains interactive elements, pressing Tab will move focus to the first component in the popover. When the popover only has non-interactive text, or when the focus is on the last component in the popover, pressing Tab will close the popover and move focus to the next tab stop on the page. The icon button trigger and interactive elements inside of the popover are in the page tab order. Use Space or Enter to open and close the popover, and use Esc or Tab on the last component to dismiss it.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (What Carbon provides > Keyboard interactions).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - The icon button has an aria-label that defines or describes what the icon is. - The button uses aria-expanded to set popover visibility and aria-controls to handle navigation to the content.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Popover
statement: A popover is a layer that pops up over all other elements on a page. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Universal behaviors Modifiers Related References Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" ().

author: IBM
title: Popover: Overview
statement: A popover is a layer that appears above all other content on the page. Only one popover can appear at a time and can contain varying text and interactive elements. Popovers are used as a base layer in some of our components like tooltips, overflow menus, and dropdown menus.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Overview).

author: IBM
title: Popover: When to use
statement: - Use when placing interactive elements, like links, buttons, or rich media to make the component more accessible. Disclosures that contain interactive elements use popovers as a base container layer to achieve this accessibility standard. For further guidance on how to display content within a popover, see the disclosure pattern. - Use when you need to display additional details for specific elements on a page. If your popover exceeds four columns in width, use a modal instead.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Overview > When to use).

author: IBM
subcategory: Popover > Overview > When not to use
title: Popover: When not to use
statement: Avoid nesting popovers or placing popovers within other popovers. This can create confusing interactions and accessibility issues. Consider using a modal or a different experience instead.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Overview > When not to use).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Variants
statement: By default, a popovers structure is made up of a container with no additional tip. Depending on the use case, caret tips or tab tips can be added to the container to help show the relationship between the popover and where it was triggered from. ; Variant ; Purpose ; ; No tip ; Popovers without a tip are typically used when the trigger button has a visually defined down state. ; Caret tip; Popovers with a caret tip should be used to help show the relationship between the popover and where it was triggered from. A caret tip is typically used when the trigger button does not have a visually defined down state and for icon buttons.; Tab tip ; Popovers can have a tab tip when the popover is connected to a toolbar or header area. ;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Overview > Variants).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Anatomy
statement: 1. UI trigger button: An interactive element that triggers the popover to open on click, hover, or focus. 2. Tip: An indicator that is added to a popover container to help show the relationship between the popover and where it was triggered from. 3. Content area: An area to place text and interactive elements. 4. Container: An area to place text and interactive elements.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Container
statement: The width and height of a popover container can vary depending on the amount of content placed within it. We recommend to not exceed a popover width size of four columns.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Formatting > Container).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Trigger button
statement: A popover is controlled by a trigger button. By default, we use an icon button to trigger a popover to open. However, as long as the trigger button is interactive it can visually change its shape and size depending on the usecase. The trigger button can open the popover on click, hover, or focus depending on what it is being used for. For more information about trigger buttons, see the disclosure pattern.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Formatting > Trigger button).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Main elements
statement: Heading, body, and footer content can vary based on your usecase. To see examples of content used in popovers, see the disclosure pattern.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Content > Main elements).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Overflow content
statement: Scrolling is usually not needed when using a popover. If scrolling is needed, in a dropdown like situation for instance, then the body section should scroll vertically with the header and footer remaining fixed in place if those elements are present. Do not scroll horizontally or let content bleed off the page.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Content > Overflow content).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Popover: No tip
statement: Popovers without a tip can be used for a wide variety of different use cases. No tip popovers are typically used when the trigger button has a visually defined down state.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (No tip).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Placement
statement: Popover directions by default are set to auto. Upon opening, popovers can detect the edges of the browser to properly be placed in view so the container does not get cutoff. Alternatively, popovers can also specify distinct directions. Direction options vary depending on the popover variant. When a popover does not have a tip, the trigger button should be flush to the side of the popover. The popover can open from the left, right, bottom, or top of the trigger button.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (No tip > Placement).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Alignment
statement: The trigger button should be placed 4px away from the popover container and should always be the same distance away from the popover container regardless of what size button is being used.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (No tip > Alignment).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Caret tip
statement: A caret tip should be added to a popover to help show the relationship between the popover and where it was triggered from. A caret tip is typically used when the trigger button does not have a visually defined down state and for icon buttons.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Caret tip).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Placement
statement: The popover can open from the left, right, bottom, or top of the trigger button. When using a caret tip, the trigger button and caret tip should be vertically centered with each other.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Caret tip > Placement).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Alignment
statement: The container of the popover may be aligned to start, center, or end to keep the container from bleeding off the page or covering important information. Similarly with no tip popovers, a trigger button paired with a caret tip popover should be placed 4px away from the popover container.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Caret tip > Alignment).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Tab tip
statement: Popovers can have a tab tip when the popover is connected to a toolbar or header area where the trigger button sits within.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Tab tip).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Placement
statement: Tab tip popovers nest within another layer on a page. The tab tip can appear on the left and right of the container and the edges should be flush with the layer edges it sits within.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Tab tip > Placement).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Alignment
statement: Popovers with a tab tip have 0px space between the trigger button and the container because they are connected to each other.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Tab tip > Alignment).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Mouse
statement: Users trigger a popover to open and close by clicking or hovering on the trigger button depending on the use case. Click: Open the popover by clicking on the trigger button. Close the popover by clicking on the trigger button again, or anywhere outside of the open popover container. Hover: Open the popover by hovering over the trigger button. Close the popover by hovering off of the popover or clicking anywhere outside of the open popover container.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Universal behaviors > Mouse).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Keyboard
statement: Focus: When the popover control has focus Enter or Space activates the popover control and toggles the visibility of the popover content.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Universal behaviors > Keyboard).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Screen readers
statement: VoiceOver: Users can trigger a button to open a popover by pressing Enter or Space while the button has focus. JAWS: Users can trigger a button to open a popover by pressing Enter or Space while the button has focus. NVDA: Users can trigger a button to open a popover by pressing Enter or Space while the button has focus.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Universal behaviors > Screen readers).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Nesting
statement: Placing one popover inside another can cause confusing interactions and accessibility issues. Consider using a modal or a different experience instead. Tooltips can be used on interactive elements within a popover, but consider their placement carefully. Ensure tooltips are positioned in a way that prevents them from being cut off within the popover container. Example of tooltip within popover
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Universal behaviors > Nesting).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Colors
statement: Popovers are most commonly used in these three different container colors—$layer-01, $layer-02, and $background-inverse.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Modifiers > Colors).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Corners
statement: A popover container has rounded corners by default and the corner radius is set to 2px. Use straight corners when the popover structure contains a tab tip and is connected to a toolbar or header to keep clean lines between the popover and the layer underneath.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Modifiers > Corners).

author: IBM
title: Popover: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Popover" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar
statement: Design annotations are needed for specific instances shown below, but for the standard progress bar component, Carbon already incorporates accessibility. What Carbon provides Design recommendations Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" ().

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via keyboard. Carbon also incorporates other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction
title: Progress bar: Keyboard interaction
statement: The progress bar itself is not keyboard operable; however, when a progress bar is active, it may temporarily disable any dependent components. For example, if a progress bar is being used to upload a file, the Upload button is disabled until the progress bar state changes to either error or completed. Progress bars are not interactive, but may temporarily disable dependent components.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > What Carbon provides > Labelling and states
title: Progress bar: Labelling and states
statement: The label above the progress bar as well as the optional helper text below it are surfaced to assistive technologies. Changes to the helper text are provided programmatically as status updates. The label, the progress bar’s status, and the optional helper text underneath are all surfaced to assistive technologies.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (What Carbon provides > Labelling and states).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Design recommendations > Provide status for indeterminate and errored progress bars
title: Progress bar: Provide status for indeterminate and errored progress bars
statement: The indeterminate progress bar does not measure progress, and so cannot programmatically inform the user when the process is complete. Also, neither variant of the progress bar can programmatically indicate to assistive technologies when it is in error. Information on both outcomes must be presented in the help text below the progress bar. Helper text is required when a progress bar is in error or indeterminate.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Design recommendations > Provide status for indeterminate and errored progress bars).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Development considerations
statement: Keep this in mind if you’re modifying Carbon or creating a custom component: - Carbon uses aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, aria-valuenow, and aria-busy to provide status on the progress bar. Due to inconsistent support for these attributes, Carbon also assigns an aria-live="polite" to the container holding the helper text. - Carbon uses aria-labelledby and aria-describedby to associate the label and helper text with the component. - The red error and green success SVG icons have aria-hidden="true" set, since the helper text and aria attributes provide the same information.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar
statement: A progress bar provides feedback about the duration and progression of a process, such as a download, file transfer, or installation, to indicate how long a user will be waiting. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Universal behaviors Modifiers Accessibility Related References Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" ().

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Overview
statement: A progress bar indicates that the user's request has been received and the application is making progress toward completing the requested action. Progress bars inform users about the status of ongoing processes, the estimated time of how long a process will take, or if a request is being executed.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Overview).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Overview > When to use
title: Progress bar: When to use
statement: - For a long operation or a process that can take a considerable or unknown amount of time - When the process can be described with quantitative information, such as a percentage - To visually show the progression of a system operation such as downloading, uploading, loading data, submitting a form, or saving updates - To convey that data is being requested, transferred, or processed
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Overview > When to use).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Overview > When not to use
title: Progress bar: When not to use
statement: - When the load time is expected to display expanded information, use skeleton states instead - When manual user actions are required to progress, use a progress indicator instead - When the progress is determined by user actions such as tutorials completed, or storage space, rather than system actions - If the process takes less than 5 seconds to load, use loading instead.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Overview > When not to use).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Variants
statement: A progress bar can either be determinate or indeterminate. The determinate variant is visualized as a track on which a bar fills up from left to right representing the progress. The indeterminate variant is visualized as a track on which a bar is moving along in constant speed, repeating over time. ; Variant ; Purpose ; ; Determinate ; Use determinate progress bars where there is clear information about the progression — they convey exact and qualitative information about the progression. ; Indeterminate; Use indeterminate progress bars where there is unclear information about the progression — they convey that users’ request, action, or data is being processed at the moment without indicating how long the activity will take.; Determinate progress bars fill from 0 to 100%. Indeterminate progress bars move along a fixed track continually until the process is complete.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Overview > Variants).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Determinate progress bar
statement: Determinate progress bars are used when the loading progress can be tracked and translated into a bar indicator which fills the track from 0% to 100% and never decreases in value or resets. Use a determinate progress bar when the progress can be calculated against a specific goal. For example, when downloading a file of a known size.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Determinate progress bar).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Indeterminate progress bar
statement: Indeterminate progress bars are used when the loading progress is unknown or the amount of wait time can't be calculated. Once triggered, the bar indicator will quickly and repeatably move from left to right (Carbon reserves back and forth motions for skeletons), while data is being gathered during the first stages of the load. In this scenario, a percentage value would not be present. This bar may change to a determinate indicator if enough information is gathered to calculate the load completion. The final determinate stage of the load is used to visually indicate the completion of the task to the user.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Indeterminate progress bar).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Indeterminate progress bar > Progress status
title: Progress bar: Progress status
statement: It's best to give the user transparency about the process which usually leads to increased trust in the software or platform. However, it may not be possible to provide progress estimation in certain cases. If progress data is not available, an indeterminate progress bar can be used. As a more concrete set of examples, there are generally three different major progressions of a system operation: downloading, uploading, and local processing.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Indeterminate progress bar > Progress status).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Indeterminate progress bar > Downloading
title: Progress bar: Downloading
statement: For downloading actions, it's usually possible to get a value of progress and update it in real time for a determinate progress bar. Depending on the information reported from a data source, time remaining could be estimated based on how much has been downloaded so far over a time period.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Indeterminate progress bar > Downloading).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Indeterminate progress bar > Uploading
title: Progress bar: Uploading
statement: Upload actions may be unable to report real time progress status depending on the data source and API configuration. However, always strive to provide users the determinate value whenever it's possible to inform them about the process.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Indeterminate progress bar > Uploading).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Indeterminate progress bar > Data processing
title: Progress bar: Data processing
statement: Data processing refers to manipulations of data to produce meaningful information. This can include currency exchange, file generation, data reformatting, or similar operations. Depending on the operation, time estimated or cycles to complete processing could be used to populate a determinate progress bar.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Indeterminate progress bar > Data processing).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Anatomy
statement: 1. Label: The text describes the process that the progress bar refers to. The label can be visually hidden, but must be defined in order to be accessible. 2. Helper text (optional, except for error): Assistive text to show additional information about the process taking place. For determinate, the text is usually a percentage, fraction, ratio, or numeric value showing progression. Such values are not applicable when a progress bar is indeterminate. A progress bar that receives an error status must convey the problem in the error helper text. 3. Track: The static area that the bar indicator moves on top of and acts as a fixed visual reference of what the total length and duration of the process could be. 4. Bar indicator: Indicates how much the process has progressed. 5. Status icon: Indicates the status of the progress bar, either in error or success status.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Height
statement: The progress bar is offered in two different sizes—big (8px) and small (4px). The big progress bar height is typically used when there is large amounts of space on a page. The small progress bar height is commonly used when space is restricted and can be placed within cards, data tables, or side panels.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Formatting > Height).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Width
statement: The width of a progress bar can vary based on the content. The minimum width of a progress bar is 48px and keep its width to a maximum of six columns when possible. If the progress bar width is too long, it can reduce readability. Don't increase the progress bar length to fill the entire width of a window or application.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Formatting > Width).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Text alignment
statement: Text alignment depends on the context and area given. Progress bar can have three ways for text alignment: default, inline, and indent. Indent alignment should only be used inside containers, tiles, or side panels which the progress bar will extend to the edges. A few common examples of text alignment for progress bars ; Text alignment; Use case ; ; Default ; Full page, cards, dialogs ; Inline ; Data table ; Indent ; Side panels, cards (usually on dashboard);
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Formatting > Text alignment).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Text placement
statement: Labels should always be placed above the progress bar for readability, and helper text below or beside. Avoid placing text inside the progress bar indicator or track. This visual could cause clutter and inconsistency in text alignment. Meanwhile, placing the text far away from the progress bar could cause confusion in the context.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Formatting > Text placement).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Internationalization (RTL)
statement: For RTL (right-to-left) languages, the layout of the progress bar is mirrored for both determinate and indeterminate options. The label is right-aligned, the value is left-aligned, and the fill progresses from right to left. Keep in mind that the placement of the percent sign differs depending on the locale.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Formatting > Internationalization (RTL)).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Content
statement: Determinate and indeterminate progress bars both have a label and an optional helper text. However, the indeterminate can’t provide the exact, quantitative information about the progression in the optional helper text.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Content).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Labels
statement: - Labels inform users what information the progress bar is processing. - Keep the label short and concise by limiting it to a few words or a single line of text. - Label text should never change as the progress bar is loading. It also does not need to be updated when the process ends, since the success or error information is provided by the bar indicator color and an icon, along with any helper text.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Content > Labels).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Helper text
statement: - Helper text is used to show additional information about the process taking place. - Common use cases of helper text for a progress bar can either be a generic phrase, for example “Fetching assets…”, or it can indicate an exact amount of something to be completed, for example "42/256 items". - When indicating a loading percentage, the percentage number should count up as the bar progresses.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Content > Helper text).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Statuses
statement: There are three statuses for the progress bar: active, success, and error. These statuses also apply on both indeterminate and determinate progress bars. After the process completes successfully or unsuccessfully, a progress bar can either remain persistent as confirmation or validation, or it can be automatically dismissed depending on what is most suitable for the use case.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Universal behaviors > Statuses).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Active
statement: The active status, represented by an animated blue bar indicator, conveys that the action is still in progress.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Universal behaviors > Active).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Success
statement: The success status, conveyed by a full-width green progress bar and checkmark icon, indicates that the action completed successfully.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Universal behaviors > Success).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Error
statement: The error status indicates that the action did not successfully complete. If an error occurs, an inline notification or error handling within the form should appear. As soon as a process fails, the indicator bar’s progress spans full width, turns red, and remains visible. A failed icon is also shown. The example shows the progress bar with error remains persistent as confirmation inside the image tile. The example shows the progress bar is automatically dismissed once it’s done uploading.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Universal behaviors > Error).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Universal behaviors > Part of a page
title: Progress bar: Part of a page
statement: While the progress bar is processing information on part of a page, you can still interact with other elements on the page. When the progress bar finishes processing it can either remain persistent on the page for confirmation or automatically dismiss itself depending on the use case. The example shows the progress bar is active and separated from other interactive elements.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Universal behaviors > Part of a page).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress bar > Universal behaviors > Inside a container
title: Progress bar: Inside a container
statement: While the progress bar is processing information that could affect multiple pieces of content within a container, such as a card, depending on the use case, the whole container should become inactive until processing has been completed or the specific section within the container being processed should become inactive until processing has been completed. The user should be able to interact with the rest of the container or page that is unaffected by the progress bar. The example shows the 'View task' action button is disabled inside the 'Tasks' container while the progress bar is active.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Universal behaviors > Inside a container).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Transitions
statement: An indeterminate bar can change to a determinate indicator (finishing from left to right) when enough information is gathered to end the load animation.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Modifiers > Transitions).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Accessibility
statement: - The loading component is implemented using the ARIA 1.1 progressbar pattern. For determinate progress bar, it outputs an ARIA role="progressbar" and uses aria-valuemin, aria-valuemax, and aria-valuenow to convey the loaded percentage to screen reader users. - If the progress bar shows the loading of a specific part or region of the application, set aria-busy="true" and aria-describedby="[progressbar-id]" on the related element to ensure assistive technologies can correctly convey this relation to the user. - Only hide the label when it is absolute clear to the user which process the progress bar represents. Note that you are still required to pass an appropriate label which will be read by screen readers.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Accessibility).

author: IBM
title: Progress bar: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress bar" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator
statement: StructuredListWrapper, StructuredListHead, StructuredListBody, StructuredListRow, StructuredListInput, StructuredListCell, OrderedList, ListItem, } from '@carbon/react'; No accessibility annotations are needed for progress indicators, but keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. Accessibility considerations Resources Accessibility testing
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" ().

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Accessibility considerations
statement: 1. Link text is the visible label for the native HTML link and is used to provide the purpose of the link which is clear and easy to understand for all users. 2. Labels are clear, concise and include the state of each step.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Accessibility considerations).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator
statement: A progress indicator guides users through any linear, multistep task by showing the user their completed, current, and future steps. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Behaviors Related Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" ().

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Overview
statement: Progress indicators help manage a user's expectations when completing a multistep process. They show which step the user is currently on, the total number of steps, and overall progress in completing a task. Example of a progress indicator used in a payment UI.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Overview).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress indicator > Overview > When to use
title: Progress indicator: When to use
statement: - When the user is working through a linear process that can be organized into three or more steps. - When the user could benefit from understanding their progress on long forms such as eCommerce checkouts, onboarding, or visa applications. - When user inputs should be validated before progressing to the next step. - To complement standard back/next navigation in a linear sequence.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Overview > When to use).

author: IBM
subcategory: Progress indicator > Overview > When not to use
title: Progress indicator: When not to use
statement: - When a process or form has fewer than three steps. - When the process may be completed in any order. - When the number of steps may change based on conditional logic.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Overview > When not to use).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Anatomy
statement: 1. Status indicator: Communicates if a step is completed, current, not started, disabled or has an error. See the status indicator pattern for guidance. 2. Active step line: Indicates completed steps and the step the user is currently on. 3. Label: Communicates what the user will accomplish in each step. Numbering each step also makes the progression more obvious. 4. Inactive step line: Indicates steps that are not started as well as steps that are in an error, disabled, or skeleton state. 5. Helper text: Labels a step as optional or in an error state.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Alignment
statement: Progress indicators can be in vertical or horizontal positions depending on the use case and the structure of the UI. When possible, arrange the progress indicator vertically for easier reading. Example of a progress indicator using vertical alignment.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Formatting > Alignment).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Placement
statement: The progress indicator component can be placed on a full page, in a modal, or in a side panel. It is also common to use the progress indicator in a tearsheet, a component provided by Carbon for IBM Products. Examples of progress indicators on a full page, tearsheet, and side panel.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Formatting > Placement).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Label
statement: The label should communicate what the user will accomplish in each step in one or two words. One option is to clearly indicate the action of the step by using the &123;verb&125; + &123;noun&125; content formula. For example, "Configure IdP" or "Define endpoints." A label may use one word if it is universally understood, such as "Cart," "Shipping," or "Payment." Avoid vague terms like "Processing." You may also number each step to make the progression more obvious.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Content > Label).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Helper text
statement: Use the helper text to indicate that a step is optional or that a step is in an error state.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Content > Helper text).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Label
statement: When there is not enough space, consider rewording the label or truncate the label text with an ellipsis and provide a tooltip to convey additional information.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Content > Label).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Helper text
statement: Long helper text may wrap to a second line, and this is preferable to truncation. Wrap the helper text beneath the label so that both maintain left alignment. Example of a helper text that wraps to the second line and maintains left alignment with the label.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Content > Helper text).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: States
statement: The progress indicator has seven states: completed, current, not started, error, disabled, hover, and focus. View the Style tab for visual specs of each state and see the status indicator pattern for additional guidance. ; State ; Description ; ; Completed ; A step is complete when a user has filled out the required information within a step and progressed to the following step. When possible, use validation to confirm that a step has been completed before the user continues. All steps that have been completed are indicated by an outlined circle with a checkmark and a blue active line.; Current ; A step is current when a user is interacting with the information within that step. The current step the user is on is indicated by a half-filled circle and a blue active line. ; Not started; A step is not started when a user has not yet interacted with that step. Steps the user has not encountered yet, or future steps, are indicated by an outlined circle and a gray active line. ; Error ; A step may be in error when a user has entered invalid or incomplete information. There could also be a server-side error. Provide clear information about the error and guidance on how to resolve the issue. ; Disabled ; A step is disabled when all interactive functions have been removed. Unlike read-only states, disabled states are not focusable, are not read by screen readers, and do not need to pass visual contrast, making them inaccessible if they need to be interpreted. ; Hover ; Use the hover state when a user's mouse cursor is hovering over the progress indicator's step. ; Focus ; When a user tabs to or clicks on the progress indicator's step, the step becomes focused, indicating the user has successfully navigated to the component. ;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Behaviors > States).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Interactions
statement: By default, the progress indicator is not interactive, providing only a visual update of the users' progress. There is also an option for an interactive progress indicator, which allows users to navigate to each step.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Behaviors > Interactions).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Mouse
statement: If the progress indicator is interactive, users can navigate to a step by clicking anywhere within the step label container.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Behaviors > Mouse).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Keyboard
statement: The first step should be selected by default. Users can navigate between steps by pressing Right or Left arrow keys. For additional keyboard interactions, see the Accessibility tab.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Behaviors > Keyboard).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Validation
statement: When possible, use validation to confirm that a step has been completed before the user continues. If any entry is invalid, the progress indicator should show an error state. Additionally, the invalid entry should be marked with an error state and include an inline error message that helps the user understand the problem and how to fix it. This kind of inline validation (or client-side validation) should happen as soon as the field loses focus. If the user cannot proceed due to a server-side issue, then an inline notification should appear. Example of a progress indicator using validation.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Behaviors > Validation).

author: IBM
title: Progress indicator: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Progress indicator" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Radio button
statement: StructuredListWrapper, StructuredListHead, StructuredListBody, StructuredListRow, StructuredListInput, StructuredListCell, OrderedList, ListItem, } from '@carbon/react'; No accessibility annotations are needed for radio buttons, but keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. What Carbon provides Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" ().

author: IBM
title: Radio button: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via the keyboard. Carbon incorporates many other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Radio button > What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction
title: Radio button: Keyboard interaction
statement: A group of radio buttons takes a single tab stop. Carbon does not require any item to be selected by default, and the first item will always take focus in case of no selection. The user changes the selected radio button using the arrow keys (up/down or left/right). Pressing Tab again will move focus out of the radio button group to the next component. A radio button group is a single tab stop and radio buttons are selected using arrow keys.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction).

author: IBM
subcategory: Radio button > What Carbon provides > Labeling and states
title: Radio button: Labeling and states
statement: Carbon surfaces the labeling of radio buttons and groups to screen readers and other assistive technologies. Carbon also provides state and context information, such as the number of items in the radio button group. JAWS screen reader output, based on the information provided by Carbon.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (What Carbon provides > Labeling and states).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Development considerations
statement: Keep this in mind if you’re modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - Carbon uses fieldset and legend to group and label sets of radio buttons. - Carbon uses label and for to programmatically connect radio buttons with their labels. - Required radio button groups must be identified programmatically, either via the label or with aria-required. - See the ARIA authoring practices for more considerations.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Radio button
statement: Use radio buttons when you have a group of mutually exclusive choices and only one selection from the group is allowed. Radio button with AI label is now stable. This addition changes the visual appearance of the component and introduces an AI explainability feature when AI is present in the component. See the AI presence section for more details. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Behaviors AI presence Related References Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" ().

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Overview
statement: Radio buttons are used for mutually exclusive choices, not for multiple choices. Only one radio button can be selected at a time. When a user chooses a new item, the previous choice is automatically deselected.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Overview).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Form
statement: Can be used in tiles, data tables, modals, side panels, and in forms on full pages.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Overview > Form).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Settings
statement: Used to change from one setting to another in a menu, page, or component. It can often act as a filtering mechanism.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Overview > Settings).

author: IBM
subcategory: Radio button > Overview > When not to use
title: Radio button: When not to use
statement: If a user can select from multiple options, use checkboxes instead of radio buttons. Radio buttons allow the user to select only one item in a set whereas checkboxes allow the user to select multiple items.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Overview > When not to use).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Anatomy
statement: The radio button component is comprised of a set of clickable circles (the inputs) with text labels positioned to the right. If there is a group of radio buttons, a group label can be added. 1. Group label (optional): Describes the group of options or provides guidance for making a selection. 2. Radio button input: Indicates the state of a radio button. By default, no option will be preselected. 3. Radio button label: Describes the information you want to select or unselect.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Alignment
statement: Radio button labels are positioned to the right of their inputs in languages that read left to right. If there is a radio button grouping, they can be laid out vertically or horizontally depending on the use case and the structure of the UI. When possible, arrange the radio button and checkbox groups vertically for easier reading. Vertically stacked versus horizontal alignment For languages that read right to left, it's acceptable to place labels to the left of the inputs. Example of radio buttons for languages that read right to left instead of left to right
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Formatting > Alignment).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Placement
statement: The radio button component is often used in forms. Forms can be placed on a full page, in a modal, or in a side panel. A radio button can also be used for changing settings in a menu or selecting a singular item in a data table. Radio buttons in a form should be placed at least 32px (layout-03) below or before the next component. Spacing of 24px (layout-02) or 16px (layout-01) can also be used when space is more restricted or if the form is more complex. For more information on spacing in forms, see our form style guidance. Spacing between a radio button and other components in a form
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Formatting > Placement).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Group labels (optional)
statement: A heading can accompany a set of radio buttons to provide further context or clarity. In some cases, a group of radio buttons may be within a larger group of components that already have a group label. In this case, an additional group label for the radio button component itself is not needed. - A group label can either state the category of the grouping or concisely instruct what actions to take below depending on the context. - Use sentence case for group labels.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Content > Group labels (optional)).

author: IBM
subcategory: Radio button > Content > Radio button labels
title: Radio button: Radio button labels
statement: - Always use clear and concise labels for radio buttons. - Labels appear to the right of radio button inputs.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Content > Radio button labels).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Overflow content
statement: - We recommend radio button labels being fewer than three words. - If you are tight on space, consider rewording the label. Do not truncate radio button label text with an ellipsis. - Long labels may wrap to a second line, and this is preferable to truncation. - Text should wrap beneath the radio button so the control and label are top aligned.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Content > Overflow content).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon's content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: States
statement: The radio button input allows for two states: unselected and selected. The default view of a radio button is having no radio button preselected. Only one radio button should be selected at a time. When a user chooses a new item, the previous choice is automatically deselected. If the user has already selected an item but wants to deselect it, consider adding alternatives such as an "other" or "none" option. In addition to unselected and selected states, radio buttons also have states for focus, disabled, read-only, error, and warning. When deciding whether to use a disabled or read-only state for radio buttons, see our Read-only states pattern guidance.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Behaviors > States).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Group states
statement: Radio button groups can receive the following states: read-only, disabled, error, and warning, as well as the addition of helper text.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Behaviors > Group states).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Mouse
statement: Users can trigger an item by clicking the radio button input directly or by clicking the radio button label. Having both regions interactive creates a more accessible click target.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Behaviors > Mouse).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Keyboard
statement: By default, no option will be preselected. Users can navigate between radio button inputs by pressing Up or Down arrow keys. If a user lands on a radio button set without a default indicator, they can press Space to select the radio button or they can press an arrow key to select the next radio button. For additional keyboard interactions, see the accessibility tab.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Behaviors > Keyboard).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: AI presence
statement: Radio button has a modification that embeds the AI label when AI present in the control. The AI variant functions the same as the normal version except with the addition of the AI label which is both a visual indicator and the trigger for the explainability popover. The AI label can be placed on the radio button group label or on individual radio button labels. For more information on designing for AI, see the Carbon for AI guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (AI presence).

author: IBM
title: Radio button: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Radio button" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Search
statement: StructuredListWrapper, StructuredListHead, StructuredListBody, StructuredListRow, StructuredListInput, StructuredListCell, OrderedList, ListItem, } from '@carbon/react'; Carbon’s search component provides the basic input mechanism for conducting a search. No accessibility annotations are needed for the input, but design annotations are needed to make the search messaging and results accessible. What Carbon provides Design recommendations Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" ().

author: IBM
title: Search: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via keyboard. Carbon also incorporates other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Search > What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction
title: Search: Keyboard interaction
statement: The search component is in the tab order, and users can type directly into the search input on focus. Users press Enter to submit their text as a search term, or they can press Esc to clear it. Once users start typing, a Cancel icon ('x') will appear, which becomes the next tab stop and provides another way to clear the input field via click, Space or Enter keys. The search input is in the tab order just like any other input. The user can clear the input by pressing Esc or activating the X button that appears inside the input. Variations of the search component use a non-persistent text input that is hidden behind a magnifying glass icon. In one variation, the user activates the icon-only button to reveal and put focus into the search input. In another variation, as the icon receives focus it exposes the input and the focus is immediately placed into the search input. Once in the input, the interaction, described above, is the same for all variations. A variation where the search input is revealed by activating the magnifying glass icon. A variation where the search input is revealed when the magnifying glass receives focus.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction).

author: IBM
subcategory: Search > What Carbon provides > Role and label
title: Search: Role and label
statement: Carbon assigns the entire search interaction a role of "search". It also provides non-visible labels for the search input and icon (“search”), and for the cancel icon (“clear search input”). The search region, input name, and clear button are all incorporated by Carbon.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (What Carbon provides > Role and label).

author: IBM
title: Search: Design recommendations
statement: Carbon provides a search pattern that outlines three search types: basic, active, and focused. Each of these types starts with the basic search input mechanism provided by Carbon’s search component. However, each search type displays suggestions or results in different ways, which all have accessibility considerations. There are three broad areas that designers need to consider and annotate for accessibility: - Search suggestions and typeahead - Search outcomes and status (e.g., “25 results found”, “no results found”) - Results navigation Future updates to this guidance will offer specific documentation on these accessibility needs.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Design recommendations).

author: IBM
title: Search: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - The div containing the search function is given a role="button". - The hidden label for the input has a default value of “search”. - The input is type="text" with a role="searchbox"; using type="search" is equivalent and also valid. - See the Mozilla search input documentation for more considerations.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Search
statement: Search enables users to specify a word or a phrase to find relevant content without navigation. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Behaviors Related Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" ().

author: IBM
title: Search: Overview
statement: Search offers users a way to explore a website or application using keywords. Search can be used as the primary means of discovering content or as a filter to aid the user in finding content.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Overview).

author: IBM
title: Search: When to use
statement: - To help users find data more efficiently within a complex or large data set. - Use at a global level when searching an entire site. - Use at a page level when searching through content on one page specifically. - Use at a component level when searching data in a component, like a data table.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Overview > When to use).

author: IBM
subcategory: Search > Overview > When not to use
title: Search: When not to use
statement: - Do not use when there is small or limited amounts of data. - Do not use when the information is simple and can be found easily within one view.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Overview > When not to use).

author: IBM
title: Search: Anatomy
statement: 1. Field: The place where a user enters their search query. 2. Search icon: Signifies a search field. The magnifying glass icon is a universal way to indicate search. 3. Field text: Inputted search text by the user. Placeholder text is visible before the user types into the field. 4. Close icon: Appears after the user has actively typed into the search field. Acts as a function to clear the search field.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Formatting > Anatomy).

author: IBM
title: Search: Styling
statement: There are two styles of search, default and fluid. They share the same functionality but look visually different, influencing where to use them. ; Style ; Appearance ; Use case ; ; Default; A traditional style where there is no label indicated. ; Use when white space is needed between components. For example, a default search style is typically used at a global or page level.; Fluid ; An alternative style where a label is placed inside of the search field and is stacked inline with the user input field text.; Use in expressive moments, fluid forms, and contained spaces. ; A default style input is shown on the top and fluid style is on the bottom.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Formatting > Styling).

author: IBM
title: Search: Default input heights
statement: There are three default search height sizes: small, medium, and large. The width varies in size based on content, layout, and design. Supporting three different search sizes gives you more flexibility when structuring layouts. ; Size ; Height (px/rem); Use case ; ; Small (sm) ; 32 / 2 ; Use when space is constricted within a design. ; Medium (md); 40 / 2.5 ; This is the default size and the most commonly used size. When in doubt, use the medium size. ; Large (lg) ; 48 / 3 ; Use when there is a lot of space to work with. The large size is typically at a global level when the user is searching content within a page view.;
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Formatting > Default input heights).

author: IBM
title: Search: Fluid input height
statement: There is only one input height at 64px and it is visually larger than the default heights.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Formatting > Fluid input height).

author: IBM
title: Search: Placement
statement: Place the search component within a user interface where users expect to find it and where it is appropriate for how it is being used in context, whether at a global level, page-specific level, or within a component. The default search can be arranged on the grid to align the container with other components containers. Search can also hang to align with other hanging component containers on the same page, depending on the use case.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Formatting > Placement).

author: IBM
title: Search: Placeholder text
statement: Useful and short text hinting at what the user can search for. For example, “Search for networks or devices.”
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Content > Placeholder text).

author: IBM
title: Search: Field text
statement: - Key words entered by the user to find a search result. - Keep the field text concise and relate the field text as closely to the result you want to find.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Content > Field text).

author: IBM
title: Search: Further guidance
statement: For further content guidance, see Carbon’s content guidelines.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Content > Further guidance).

author: IBM
title: Search: States
statement: The search component has four states: enabled, focus, filled, and disabled.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Behaviors > States).

author: IBM
title: Search: Mouse
statement: Click on the search field input to start typing. Once a user starts typing, a close icon (‘x’) will appear and provides a way to clear the input field by clicking on the Close icon.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Behaviors > Mouse).

author: IBM
title: Search: Keyboard
statement: Press Enter to submit text as a search term, or press Esc to clear the search field. Once a user starts typing, a Close icon (‘x’) will appear and provides a way to clear the input field by pressing the Spaceor Enter keys.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Behaviors > Keyboard).

author: IBM
title: Search: Feedback
statement: Help us improve this component by providing feedback, asking questions, and leaving any other comments on GitHub.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Search" (Feedback).

author: IBM
title: Select
statement: StructuredListWrapper, StructuredListHead, StructuredListBody, StructuredListRow, StructuredListInput, StructuredListCell, OrderedList, ListItem, } from '@carbon/react'; No accessibility annotations are needed for selects, but keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. What Carbon provides Development considerations
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Select" ().

author: IBM
title: Select: What Carbon provides
statement: Carbon bakes keyboard operation into its components, improving the experience of blind users and others who operate via keyboard. Carbon also incorporates other accessibility considerations, some of which are described below.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Select" (What Carbon provides).

author: IBM
subcategory: Select > What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction
title: Select: Keyboard interaction
statement: A select component is reached by Tab and opened with Space, or the Up or Down arrow keys. The currently selected option will have focus. The arrow keys are also used for navigating between options. Users can jump about in the list by pressing individual letter keys, which will reposition to the first option beginning with that letter. Options are selected with Space or Enter keys, which also close the select. Pressing Esc closes a select without changing the selected option. Selects are reached by Tab. Space and arrow keys open the list of options. The arrow keys navigate the open list of options, with the Space or Enter keys selecting the option with focus and closing the list. Esc closes the list without changing the option.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Select" (What Carbon provides > Keyboard interaction).

author: IBM
title: Select: Development considerations
statement: Keep these considerations in mind if you are modifying Carbon or creating a custom component. - Carbon uses the combined attributes disabled, hidden, and selected in order to make a default prompt such as “Choose an option” not appear in the list of options when the select is open. - The component is built on the HTML select element and has limited styling, with most of the visual appearance coming from the browser.
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Select" (Development considerations).

author: IBM
title: Select
statement: Select allows users to choose one option from a list of values. Select with AI label is now stable. This addition changes the visual appearance of the component and introduces an AI explainability feature when AI is present in the component. See the AI presence section for more details. Live demo Overview Formatting Content Universal behaviors AI presence Related Feedback
citation: IBM. IBM Carbon Design System: "Select" ().

author: IBM
title: Select: Overview
